answer.rationale: Constraints first: rollback is off the table (compliance bars reverting the security patch), so memory_b1 and memory_b6 are informative but unusable here. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fail fast by shedding requests — at settlement peak on a write-heavy path that directly contradicts the 'without losing customer writes' objective. Added capacity (memory_b3) worked when it was provisioned *ahead* of a known peak; provisioning mid-incident is unlikely to land inside the 90-minute degradation window. Regional failover (memory_b2) is the strongest match to the 'confined to the primary region' signal, but the archived record describes a latency degradation and says nothing about replication lag or write durability during a heavy-write peak — shifting the write path under load is the one option that can lose committed-but-unreplicated writes. So I hold it as the escalation, not the first move. That leaves read-replica routing (memory_b5), which is reversible, adds no write-loss exposure, and plausibly attacks the same mechanism (read contention on the primary starving write throughput). I spend the single verification on memory_b5 rather than memory_b2 because b5 is the memory I intend to act on and its causal claim is the weakest link: 'write latency recovered the same day' is loose attribution, and I need to know whether the original incident was write-heavy at peak or a quiet-period dashboard problem. If the source shows it was a low-write window, the read-offload lever probably will not move a 5x write p99 and I should escalate to guarded regional failover with an explicit replication-lag check in the next window. Running this at small guarded scale: shift a bounded slice of report/read traffic off the primary, watch write p99 and queue depth for a short interval, and keep failover staged behind it. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: whether the new release itself is the root cause, since I cannot revert it to test that — read offload may only mask a regression that will resurface.
